n: Next Israel turned north toward Bashan, and King Og came out to fight at Edrei.

f.g: A fertile plateau east of the Sea of Galilee.

n: The Lord told Moses not to fear, for He would give Og into their hands like Sihon.
The Lord delivered Og and his people completely.
Israel captured all sixty cities of the region of Argob, Og’s kingdom.

f.g: threescore = sixty
A district within Bashan, perhaps meaning “stony.”

n: These were fortified cities with high walls, gates, and bars, plus many unwalled villages. The fortresses the spies had feared proved no match for God.

f.g: Fortified.
Heavy beams used to bolt city gates.

n: They devoted these cities to destruction as they had with Sihon.

f.g: Devoted wholly to God (ḥerem), usually by destruction.

n: The livestock and goods were kept as plunder.
Israel now held the land east of the Jordan from the Arnon River up to Mount Hermon.

f.g: The tall, snow-capped mountain at Israel’s far north (about 9,200 feet).

n: A note on names: the Sidonians called Hermon “Sirion,” and the Amorites “Shenir.”
This included the plateau towns, all of Gilead, and all of Bashan.

f.g: The high tableland (mishor) north of the Arnon.

n: Og was the last of the Rephaim, an ancient race of giants. His huge iron (or basalt) bed — about 13 feet long and 6 feet wide — was still displayed in Rabbah of Ammon.

f.g: Hebrew Rephaim — an ancient people remembered for great size.
Possibly a bed of dark basalt, which looks like iron, or a coffin-like couch.
Rabbah, capital of Ammon — modern Amman, Jordan.

n: Moses gave the land from Aroer to half of Gilead to Reuben and Gad.
The rest of Gilead and all of Bashan went to the half tribe of Manasseh.
Jair of Manasseh took the Argob region and named its villages after himself, Havvoth-jair.

f.g: Small Aramean kingdoms north of Bashan.

n: Gilead was given to Machir, the Manassite clan that had conquered it (Numbers 32:39-40).
Reuben and Gad received the land from Gilead to the Arnon and up to the Jabbok, Ammon’s border.
Also the Jordan valley from the Sea of Galilee to the Dead Sea, below the slopes of Pisgah.

f.g: The Sea of Galilee.
The slopes of Pisgah.

n: Moses reminded these tribes that, though they had their land, their fighting men must cross over armed with their brothers.

f.g: meet = fit, suitable

f.w: pass over armed before your brethren

n: Their families and herds could stay in the eastern cities.
Only after the Lord gave rest to all Israel west of the Jordan could they return home. Brotherhood meant finishing the work together.

f.g: Peace and security in the land.

n: Moses encouraged Joshua: you have seen what God did to these two kings; He will do the same to every kingdom you face.
Do not fear them, for the Lord Himself fights for you.
Moses now shares a personal moment: he pleaded with the Lord.

f.g: besought = begged, pleaded

n: He praised God: You have only begun to show me Your greatness. What god in heaven or earth can do such works?

f.g: Hebrew Adonai YHWH — “Lord Jehovah.”

f.w: what God is there in heaven or in earth

n: Moses asked to cross over and see the good land — “that goodly mountain” and Lebanon. After forty years of leading, he longed to finish the journey.

f.g: The fine hill country of Canaan.

n: But the Lord, angry “for your sakes,” said, “Enough — speak no more of this.” Even a great prophet received a “no” to a heartfelt prayer.

f.g: “That is enough for you.”

n: Instead, God let Moses climb Pisgah and view the land in every direction. A gift within the disappointment.
Moses must charge, encourage, and strengthen Joshua, who would lead Israel in. Moses’ last work was preparing his successor.
So Israel stayed in the valley across from Beth-peor — the place of their recent sin, and where Moses would later be buried.
